In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel approach for real-time traffic classification that can be deployed on commodity hardware, with no need for specialized network cards.

a novel combination of techniques that can be used to efficiently classify network traffic in the presence of high packet rates, with the ultimate goal to enable real-time traffic analysis in large-scale networks.
the design of an efficient and scalable software-based traffic classification solution, and the implementation of the proposed techniques in a real-world system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have achieved a significant breakthrough in the performance and efficiency of traffic classification engines running on commodity hardware.
the proposed system is able to process 14.2Mpps of packets over a single 1Gbps link, and up to 14Gbps of traffic when using 10Gbps links.
we are able to achieve a classification rate of about 14.2 Gbps on a commodity server, which is about 10 times faster than any previous software implementation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, by using commodity multi-core hardware (Intel Xeon E5520 @ 2.27 GHz) and a single 10 Gigabit NIC, we are able to perform real-time statistical classification of network flows at wire speed, i.e., at a rate of 14.2Mpps.
we have achieved a 10x improvement in classification rates with respect to the previous state of the art, while maintaining an accuracy of 99.5%.
the presented system can process up to 14 Mpps of 64-byte packets, and up to 2.5 Mpps of 1518-byte packets, with an average classification rate of 95% on 10 Gbps links.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, by carefully exploiting the available resources of a commodity hardware, it is possible to build a software-based traffic classifier able to operate at wire speed.
commodity hardware is already powerful enough to enable the real-time processing of large volumes of network data.

commodity network hardware can be leveraged to perform real-time statistical classification of network flows, even when the traffic mix includes protocols that cannot be classified with high precision.
